title: Spotting fake photos, videos and voices
essentialQuestion: How can you tell if a photo, video or voice is real?
learningGoal: Explain how AI can make realistic pictures, videos and voices, and check the source before you trust or share one.

warmUp.question: You see a photo of a pumpkin as big as a car. What do you think first?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: Who posted each one? What can you check? Which ones can you not tell yet?

cards.title: Posts in the Greenhill news group

cases.name: Post A: a giant pumpkin
cases.body: A photo of a pumpkin as big as a car, posted by a page with no name. The Greenhill farm's own page says it grew no giant pumpkin this year. The farmer's hand in the photo looks a little odd.

cases.name: Post B: a talking goat
cases.body: A video of a goat that says “Good morning” in clear words. The Greenhill comedy club posted it. The caption says: “Made with AI, just for fun.”

cases.name: Post C: rain at the market
cases.body: A photo of the market in heavy rain, posted by the market's own page this morning. Other people posted photos of the same rain.

cases.name: Post D: a voice message
cases.body: A voice message that sounds like Coach Ana. It says: “The football game moves to six in the morning.” It came from a number nobody knows. The notice board at the centre still says four in the afternoon.

cases.name: Post E: a cat on a roof
cases.body: A photo of a cat asleep on a roof. Nothing looks strange. There is no name and no date.

cases.name: Post F: a fruit seller
cases.body: A photo of a fruit seller. Her skin looks very smooth, and the background is blurry. The Greenhill photo club posted it with the photographer's name, and says it was taken with a phone in the evening.

activity.title: Check each post
activity.instructions: Put each Greenhill post in a group. There is no score. After you place a post, you can see one possible answer and the reason.

groups.label: Made with AI, and it says so

items.feedback: The farm's own page says it grew no giant pumpkin, and the page that posted it has no name. The odd hand is only a reason to check. Real photos can look odd too.
The comedy club says clearly that it used AI, for fun. That is not a trick. It would become one if someone shared it without the label, as if it were real.

items.text: Post C: rain at the market
items.feedback: It comes from the market's own page, and other people show the same rain.
It sounds like Coach Ana, but it came from an unknown number. The notice board says something else. Ask her in person, or call her usual number.

items.text: Post E: a cat on a roof
items.feedback: Nothing looks strange, but a new fake can look perfect. With no name and no date, you can't check the source yet. “Probably real” can make sense too, if you give a reason.
The photo club says who took it and how. Real phone photos can look smooth and blurry too, in the evening.

activity.saves: The group the learner chose for each post, with the lesson's other answers. Group ids real, fake and check are unchanged from the first draft; labelled is new.
activity.offline: Everything is in the lesson file. The posts are short descriptions (and, later, simple drawings); there are no real photos, videos or sounds, and nothing is sent anywhere.

sections.heading: AI can make pictures, videos and voices
sections.text: Some AI tools can create new pictures, videos and voices. These tools learned from enormous numbers of real examples, so what they make can look and sound realistic. Many people use these tools openly for art, films or education, and explain that AI made the work. A fake is different: it pretends to show something real that never happened. A deepfake is a fake that copies a real person's face or voice, often to trick people for money or attention. In Greenhill, the comedy club posted a talking goat with the label “Made with AI, just for fun”. Someone else posted a photo of a pumpkin as big as a car. Is it real?
sections.simpler: Some AI tools make new pictures, videos and voices. They learned from lots of real examples. So the new ones look realistic. Some people say openly that AI made their art or lessons. A fake is different. It shows something that never happened, as if it were real. A deepfake copies a real person's face or voice to trick people. In Greenhill, the comedy club's talking goat says AI made it. But is the huge pumpkin real?

sections.heading: Strange details are clues, not proof
sections.text: AI pictures sometimes have small mistakes, such as an extra finger, messy letters on a sign or a background that melts into a wall. In a video, the mouth may not move with the words. These details can be clues, but they are not proof. Newer tools make fewer mistakes, so a fake can look perfect. Real photographs can also look strange, for example when they are blurry or taken in poor light. In a 2025 study, participants wrongly labelled about one in four real photographs as AI-made. The fruit seller's photo has very smooth skin, but the photo club says a phone took it.
sections.simpler: AI pictures sometimes have mistakes, like six fingers or messy letters. These are clues. But clues are not proof. New tools make fewer mistakes. Real photos can look strange too, when they are dark or not sharp. In a 2025 study, people looked at real photos. They called about one in four of them AI-made. The fruit seller has very smooth skin. But a phone took that photo.

sections.heading: Check the source
sections.text: The most useful check is the source. Who posted it, and when? Can you find where it first came from? Do other trusted sources show the same thing? The farm's own page says it grew no giant pumpkin, so that photo is probably fake. The rain photo came from the market's own page, and other people posted the same rain, so it is probably real. For a voice message, contact the person in another way. Coach Ana's message came from an unknown number, so ask her in person. If you still can't tell, say so, and don't share it yet.
sections.simpler: So check the source. Who posted it? When? Where did it come from first? Do people you trust show the same thing? The farm says it has no giant pumpkin. So that photo is probably fake. The rain photo came from the market itself. Others posted the same rain. Coach Ana's message came from a number nobody knows. So ask her in person. Not sure? Don't share it yet.

glossary.definition: Looking or sounding like the real thing.
glossary.example: The pumpkin photo looks realistic at first.

glossary.definition: Made to look real, but it is not real.
glossary.example: The pumpkin photo is probably a fake.

glossary.definition: A fake picture, video or voice that copies a real person, made with AI.
glossary.example: A deepfake of Coach Ana's voice could trick the football team.

glossary.definition: A small sign that helps you find out something.
glossary.example: An extra finger is a clue to check a picture. It is not proof.

glossary.definition: The person or place that information comes from.
glossary.example: The farm's own page is a good source about its pumpkins.

checks.question: What is the best reason to think the pumpkin photo is fake?

options.text: The farm says it grew no giant pumpkin
options.feedback: Yes. The farm is the best source about its own pumpkins, and the page that posted the photo has no name.

options.text: The farmer's hand in the photo looks a bit odd
options.feedback: Not quite. An odd hand is a reason to check, not proof. Real photos can look odd too. Read the second section.

options.text: The pumpkin in the photo is a very bright orange
options.feedback: Not quite. Real pumpkins are orange too. Read about checking the source in the third section.

checks.question: A voice message sounds just like Coach Ana. What is the best thing to do?

options.text: Share it with the whole team now
options.feedback: Not quite. AI can copy a voice, so it may not be her. Read the third section.

options.text: Trust it because it sounds like her
options.feedback: Not quite. Sounding real is not proof. Read about voice messages in the third section.

options.text: Ask Coach Ana in person first
options.feedback: Yes. Checking with the person in another way is the best test for a voice message.

checks.question: Why is a strange detail in a picture not enough to prove it is fake?
checks.placeholder: It is not enough because ... So I should also ...

write.prompt: Choose one post from the Greenhill news group. Say which group you put it in, and explain how you checked it or would check it.
selfCheck: I named one post and the group I chose.
I gave a reason from the post.
I said how I would check the source.
write.example: I chose Post A, the giant pumpkin. I put it in “Probably fake” because the farm's own page says it grew no giant pumpkin this year. The source is a page with no name, so I can't see who made it. The farmer's hand looks odd, but that is only a reason to check, because real photos can look odd too. To check it, I would also ask someone at the market. Before I share it, I would wait until I know more.

speak.partnerTask: Your partner picks a Greenhill post. You choose a group, give one reason, and say how you would check it. Then switch.
speak.independentTask: Say out loud three ways to check a picture, video or voice. Then say why a strange detail is not proof.

watch.title: AI Unlocked: Recognizing AI-generated content
watch.why: It was made with teenage fact-checkers, and it shows the clues in AI-made pictures, videos and voices.
watch.beforeQuestion: What do you think a fake video might get wrong?
watch.afterQuestion: Why is it not enough to trust a tool that says if something is fake?
watch.summary: This video comes from a series made with a team of teenage fact-checkers. It explains that some people use AI to make fake pictures, videos and sounds. They often do it to get money, attention or power. The video shows clues to look for. AI pictures can have strange hands, odd shadows and strange backgrounds. In AI videos, look for edges that blur or flicker. Check the shadows, and check if the lips move with the words. For AI voices, listen to the tone and to the sounds in the background. The video also shows tools that can help, like a search that finds where else a picture appears online. But these tools are not always right. A person still needs to think and check before sharing.
keyPoints: AI fakes can have clues: odd hands, shadows, backgrounds, edges or lips.
For a voice, listen to the tone and the background sounds.
Tools that spot fakes are not always right, so a person still needs to check.
watch.contentNote: Fast American English with real examples of AI-made content. It mentions tools that need the internet (reverse image search and AI detection apps); on an offline device, learners can ask a teacher instead. The summary was written from PBS NewsHour Classroom's lesson plan for this video, not from watching it. Preview it first; learners can read the written summary instead.

sensitiveNotes: Deepfakes are used to hurt real people: fake pictures that shame someone, fake videos of leaders, and cloned voices in scams (for example a call that sounds like a relative asking for money; see the FTC source). The lesson keeps its examples silly on purpose. Don't show real deepfakes of real people in class. If a learner says a fake was made of them or someone they know, don't discuss the details in class; follow the partner's own safeguarding process.
educatorNotes: Teach checking first: who posted it, when, where it first came from, whether other trusted sources show the same thing, and for a voice, contacting the person another way. Visual glitches (extra fingers, messy letters, smooth skin) are reasons to check, never proof: newer tools make fewer of them, and real photos can show odd details too. In a 2025 study (Kamali and others, CHI '25), people correctly called real photographs real 74% of the time, so about one in four were wrongly called AI-made. Accept “can't tell yet” as a strong answer; the activity has no score. Paper version: the six posts on cards, sorted under the four headings.

Labelled AI work (art, films, lessons, a joke clearly marked “Made with AI”) is not the same as a fake that pretends to be real or copies a real person. Labels can be lost when a picture is reposted (News Literacy Project, 2026), so a labelled post can become misleading when shared without it. In Indonesia, Mafindo's TurnBackHoax and CekFakta check viral pictures and videos, and Mafindo says AI-based hoaxes are getting harder to tell apart (Liputan6, 2026). A teacher with internet can show one checked example; learners don't need to go online.

Revised on 1 November 2026 from Justin's review: checking the source is now the core skill (who posted it, when, where it first came from, who else shows it, and asking the person another way for a voice); visual glitches are taught as clues to check, never proof, with a dated study showing people call about one in four real photos AI-made (Kamali and others, CHI '25), and the evidence, activity, quick check, Write example and Speak no longer reward spotting fingers or skin. A new group, “Made with AI, and it says so”, separates labelled creative work (the comedy club's goat) from deceptive fakes and deepfakes; Post F is now a real photo that only looks odd. Feedback gives the reason, not “what most people would say”. The evidence stays fully fictional; the real study is in the reading, the teacher notes and sources (the News Literacy Project lesson plan and MIT Detect Fakes sources were replaced by sources opened for this revision). Title unchanged; “Checking photos, videos and voices” would fit the lesson better (for Nick and Justin to decide).
